sections.heading: Planning a deck and a fence for the same yard
paragraphs: If you want both, plan them together, even if one gets built months after the other. The deck stairs decide where people step into the yard, and that path usually ends at a gate. A fence line drawn on its own can put the gate far from where the stairs come down. Sketch both on one drawing of the lot so the gate sits on the path you will actually walk.

In many yards the deck goes in first. Deck lumber and the equipment for digging footings have to reach the backyard, and they usually come through a side yard. Once a fence closes that side, everything has to fit through the gate. If the fence has to come first, say because a dog needs a yard now, plan a gate wide enough for materials or leave one section open until the deck is done. A drive gate often handles this, and it stays useful later for a mower or a trailer.

sections.heading: Choosing materials and heights that work together
paragraphs: The deck and the fence do not need to be the same material, but they should look planned. Cedar and pressure treated pine weather differently, so a cedar fence beside a pine deck can drift apart in color after a few summers. Using the same stain on both helps, though the two woods take stain a little differently, so test it on a scrap of each first. Composite deck boards come in set colors and generally are not stained. With composite, pick a fence stain close to the deck color instead of chasing an exact match.

Height deserves a look as well. A raised deck puts you above the yard, and a privacy fence of the usual height may not block the view from the deck into the yard next door. When privacy up on the deck matters, a screen along one side of the deck often does more than a taller fence. Fence height is also limited by many cities and HOAs. Our [deck page](/decks/) and [fence page](/fences/) go deeper on each one.

sections.heading: What to have ready before we look at the yard
paragraphs: Photos help with what cannot be seen on a dry afternoon. A picture taken after a hard rain shows where water sits, which matters for footings and for the bottom of a fence. Find your survey or plat too. It shows where the lot lines run and whether an easement crosses the yard, and it often came with the closing papers when you bought the house. The guide on [fences and property lines](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) explains why the lines come first.

In an HOA, pull the covenants and the architectural guidelines before the visit, and find out how the committee wants requests sent in. Knowing the limits on fence height and stain color early keeps the plan from being drawn twice. It also helps to note anything buried that utility locators usually do not mark, like sprinkler lines or a septic field. For the submission itself, see the [HOA approval guide](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/).

faqs.q: Do you build both decks and fences?
faqs.a: Yes, we build both, and one request covers them. In the estimate form below, choose Both as the project type and use the notes to describe each part, even roughly. Planning them in one conversation makes it easier to line up the deck stairs with a gate and to pick finishes that suit each other.

We work across Middle Tennessee. Each city we serve has its own page covering the ground and local rules there, and you can find them all on our [service areas page](/service-areas/). If your town is missing from that list, the ZIP code field in the estimate form is how we check whether your address falls inside the area we cover.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a deck or a fence?
faqs.a: Decks need one more often than fences do. A deck attached to the house or built high off the ground typically goes through a permit and inspections. Fence rules differ more from town to town, and some places do not ask for a fence permit at all. HOA approval is a separate step either way. Check with the city or county codes office for your address, and see our [deck permit guide](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) for how the process usually works.

faqs.q: How do I get an estimate?
faqs.a: Start with the form at the bottom of this page. Pick the kind of project and add your ZIP code so we can confirm your address is in our area. The notes box is for anything else we should know, like an old fence or deck that has to come out first. After that, we set a time to see the yard, and the estimate follows once we have walked the space with you.
